sections.title: What is a Heap?
sections.content:
A heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the **heap property**: in a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children, so the root always holds the minimum. In a max-heap every parent is ≥ its children.

The complete binary tree structure lets a heap be stored in an array without pointers. Node at index `i` has left child `2i+1`, right child `2i+2`, parent `Math.floor((i-1)/2)`.

Heaps power **priority queues** — dequeue always returns the highest-priority item. When the problem says 'always give me the cheapest/fastest/most frequent next item', you want a heap.

JS has no built-in heap. Implement a min-heap from scratch (~25 lines) or simulate with a sorted array for small n. Sorted array gives O(n) insert vs O(log n) for a real heap.

Three canonical patterns: **Top K elements** (min-heap of size K), **Merge K sorted lists** (heap with one entry per list), **Median of a stream** (two-heap split).

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Reach for a heap when you need to repeatedly extract the minimum or maximum from a dynamically changing set. Sorting gives a one-shot answer; heaps handle dynamic insertions in O(log n) per operation.

sections.title: Heap Structure and Core Operations
sections.content:
## Array Index Math

Parent of i: `Math.floor((i-1)/2)`. Left child: `2i+1`. Right child: `2i+2`.

## Insert — Bubble Up

Append element, compare with parent, swap if out of order, repeat until heap property holds. O(log n).

## Extract Min — Bubble Down

Swap root with last element, remove last, bubble down new root: swap with smaller child, repeat. O(log n).

## Build Heap in O(n)

Floyd's heapify: call bubbleDown on every non-leaf from `Math.floor(n/2)-1` down to 0. O(n) due to geometric series of work per level.

## Top K Pattern

Min-heap of size K: push each element, if size > K pop the minimum. After all elements, heap contains the K largest. O(n log K).

## K-Way Merge

Min-heap with one entry per list storing `(value, listIndex, position)`. Extract min → add to result → push next from that list. O(N log K).

sections.title: Decrease-Key and Indexed Priority Queues
sections.content:
A plain heap supports insert and extract-min/max, but NOT an efficient 'decrease the priority of an element already in the heap' - which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm needs every time it finds a shorter path to an already-queued node. JavaScript's built-in structures don't offer a true decrease-key heap, so two practical workarounds are used instead:

**Lazy deletion (the common workaround)**: instead of decreasing a key in place, just push a new entry with the better priority, leaving the stale old entry in the heap. When popping, check if the popped entry is stale (compare against a separately-tracked best-known distance); if so, discard it and pop again. This is simpler to implement than a true indexed heap and is what almost all interview-level Dijkstra's implementations actually do - the heap can hold up to O(E) entries instead of O(V), but this doesn't change the O(E log E) = O(E log V) overall complexity.

**True indexed heap**: maintain a separate `position` array mapping each element to its current index in the heap array, updated on every swap during bubble-up/bubble-down. `decreaseKey` then looks up the element's position in O(1) and bubbles it up directly, avoiding the duplicate-entries approach entirely. More complex to implement correctly, but keeps the heap at exactly O(V) entries - worth knowing this exists, even though lazy deletion is the more common interview answer.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Array-based min-heap with O(log n) push/pop. topK demonstrates the min-heap of size K pattern for finding K largest elements.

items.name: Max-Heap
items.description: Invert all comparisons in _up and _down. Root holds maximum. Use for 'K smallest' by maintaining a max-heap of size K and evicting the maximum.
items.example_problem: Kth Largest Element in an Array

items.name: Two-Heap (Median Maintenance)
items.description: Max-heap for the lower half and min-heap for the upper half, sizes balanced to differ by at most 1. Median is top of larger heap or average of both tops. O(log n) per insertion.

items.name: Heap with Custom Comparator
items.description: For (frequency, value) pairs, store tuples and compare on the first element. Extend MinHeap with a comparator function passed to the constructor.

items.name: K-Way Merge with Heap
items.description: Initialize heap with first element of each list. Each pop gives the globally next smallest element; push the next element from that list. O(N log K) total.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: Insert and delete traverse one root-to-leaf path of height log2(n). Peek reads index 0. Floyd's heapify builds from n elements in O(n). Space is O(n) for the array with no pointer overhead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using a min-heap for 'top K largest' seems backward but is correct — you evict the smallest, keeping the K largest. A max-heap of size K would require draining the whole heap at the end.
JS has no built-in heap — a sorted array gives O(n) insert, turning O(n log K) into O(n^2). Fine for n < 1000, catastrophic for n = 10^6.
Forgetting n < K edge case — when the array has fewer than K elements, return all of them.
Floyd's heapify is O(n); inserting n elements one-by-one is O(n log n). Use heapify only when the full array is known upfront.
Parent index off-by-one: Math.floor((i-1)/2) not Math.floor(i/2) for 0-indexed arrays.
